5:30Before the day begins

Let me take you back to this morning

The street is still quiet and the kettle has just boiled. Before the day begins, here’s a little about the person who’d be caring for your clients.

Support worker by profession

I hold a Certificate III in Individual Support (Ageing and Disability) and have worked as a full support worker at St Vincent’s Aged Care in Sydney. Personal care, medication assistance, meals, safe transfers, community outings and clear progress notes are part of my everyday practice.

A support plan tells me what someone needs. I take the time to learn the rest: how they like their tea, the stories they love to tell, and what helps them feel safe. That’s what turns good care into care people look forward to.

Patient by nature

My path into care began behind a shop counter. In more than three years at Woolworths, first in Caringbah and now in Hobart, I learned to slow down for the shopper who needs extra time and to really listen to the person who simply wants a friendly chat. Those habits come with me into every home and every room.

My cyber and network security studies at TAFE NSW mean I treat private information with care and pick up care software quickly. Hobart is now my home, I volunteer with the Australian Red Cross, and I’m committed to supporting this community for the long term.

Good care is noticing the small things. The cold room, the quieter voice, the cup of tea that hasn’t been touched.

A promise I bring to everyone I support

12:30A quiet lunch break, and a look back

The places that taught me to care

Each role has added something to the way I care. Open one to see what I bring from it.

This is where my training became real. Every resident had their own routine and their own way of telling me what they needed. I learned to observe closely, listen well and be a dependable part of a busy care team.

  • Delivered personal care (showering, hygiene, grooming, dressing and continence) in line with individual support plans, protecting each person’s privacy and dignity.
  • Assisted clients with medication in line with care plans and organisational policy.
  • Provided domestic assistance and meal preparation, keeping living spaces safe, clean and comfortable.
  • Supported community access, including shopping, appointments and outings, encouraging inclusion and independence.
  • Performed safe manual handling and transfers, and reassured people living with dementia through familiar routines and patient communication.
  • Noticed and escalated changes in health, mood and behaviour, and recorded clear, timely care notes.

Thousands of everyday conversations taught me to read people kindly and treat everyone with the same respect. Through more than three years and a move interstate, I’ve remained a trusted part of the team.

  • Assist diverse customers every day, including older and vulnerable shoppers, with patience, respect and clear communication.
  • Transferred from the Caringbah store to Hobart in July 2026, and still part of the team today.

Volunteering keeps me close to my community, and quietly reminds me why this work matters.

  • Support the Red Cross retail team, welcoming customers and helping the store run smoothly.
14:00The unexpected moments

When the day doesn’t go to plan

No plan can predict every moment. Here’s how I respond calmly and safely when the day changes, guided by my training, my experience and each person’s support plan.

A client says no to their shower this morning.

Choice, control and dignity

How I’d help

  1. Accept their answer calmly. It’s their body and their choice, and trust matters more than a timetable.
  2. Gently ask what’s behind it. They might be cold, tired, sore, rushed or anxious.
  3. Offer choices that suit them, like a later time, a wash at the basin or a warmer room.
  4. Note it in my care notes, and let my supervisor know if it keeps happening.

A resident living with dementia is upset and asking to go home.

Dementia care and communication

How I’d help

  1. Stay calm, soften my voice and come down to their eye level.
  2. Comfort the feeling rather than correct it: “You’re missing home. Tell me about it.”
  3. Check gently for a need underneath, like pain, hunger, thirst or the toilet.
  4. Ease them into a familiar routine from their support plan, and note what helped.

A client is much quieter than usual and hasn’t touched lunch.

Noticing and escalating changes

How I’d help

  1. Sit with them for a moment and kindly ask how they’re feeling.
  2. Look for signs like pain, confusion, fever, breathing changes or a fall they haven’t mentioned.
  3. Tell the nurse or supervisor straight away, following the escalation procedure.
  4. Write down exactly what I noticed, with times, so the next worker can follow up.
